statement: Net transmembrane current of one pyramidal cell during a synaptic burst, used as the slider default: dipole moment ÷ sink–source separation ≈ 0.5 pA·m ÷ 0.5 mm ≈ 1 nA (derived from the cited moment and length; a single synapse carries ~100 pA).
sources: Murakami S, Okada Y (2006). Contributions of principal neocortical neurons to magnetoencephalography and electroencephalography signals. Journal of Physiology 575(3):925–936 doi:10.1113/jphysiol.2006.105379
Galloni AR, Laffere A, Rancz E (2020). Apical length governs computational diversity of layer 5 pyramidal neurons. eLife 9:e55761 doi:10.7554/eLife.55761

Markram H, Lübke J, Frotscher M, Roth A, Sakmann B (1997). Physiology and anatomy of synaptic connections between thick tufted pyramidal neurones in the developing rat neocortex. Journal of Physiology 500(Pt 2):409–440 doi:10.1113/jphysiol.1997.sp022031

statement: In realistic compartmental models a layer-5 pyramidal cell produces a current dipole of 0.41–0.90 pA·m during the slow envelope of a burst (spikes −0.78 to +2.97 pA·m); a layer-2/3 pyramidal cell 0.29 pA·m (envelope) and 0.47 pA·m (spike).
sources: Murakami S, Okada Y (2006). Contributions of principal neocortical neurons to magnetoencephalography and electroencephalography signals. Journal of Physiology 575(3):925–936 doi:10.1113/jphysiol.2006.105379

statement: A routinely measured MEG/EEG source has an equivalent current dipole of about 10 nA·m, caused by the synchronous activity of tens of thousands of neurons; pyramidal-cell bursts become detectable when 10,000–50,000 cells are synchronously active.
sources: Hämäläinen M, Hari R, Ilmoniemi RJ, Knuutila J, Lounasmaa OV (1993). Magnetoencephalography—theory, instrumentation, and applications to noninvasive studies of the working human brain. Reviews of Modern Physics 65(2):413–497 doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.65.413

Murakami S, Okada Y (2006). Contributions of principal neocortical neurons to magnetoencephalography and electroencephalography signals. Journal of Physiology 575(3):925–936 doi:10.1113/jphysiol.2006.105379

statement: Inhibitory synaptic currents also generate substantial transmembrane currents; spike-triggered unitary field potentials in human and monkey cortex indicate that the LFP reflects primarily inhibitory-neuron activity (by timing; amplitudes of inhibitory and excitatory unitary fields did not differ significantly).
sources: Buzsáki G, Anastassiou CA, Koch C (2012). The origin of extracellular fields and currents — EEG, ECoG, LFP and spikes. Nature Reviews Neuroscience 13(6):407–420 doi:10.1038/nrn3241

Teleńczuk B, Dehghani N, Le Van Quyen M, Cash SS, Halgren E, Hatsopoulos NG, Destexhe A (2017). Local field potentials primarily reflect inhibitory neuron activity in human and monkey cortex. Scientific Reports 7:40211 doi:10.1038/srep40211

statement: Dura mater conductivity used in a dura-inclusive finite-element head model is 0.06 S/m (bounds 0.02–0.1 S/m, about 0.04× CSF); the meta-analysis found insufficient data for dura. Including the dura layer reduced simulated scalp potentials by about 20% (up to 40% at the peak location).
sources: Ramon C, Garguilo P, Fridgeirsson EA, Haueisen J (2014). Changes in scalp potentials and spatial smoothing effects of inclusion of dura layer in human head models for EEG simulations. Frontiers in Neuroengineering 7:32 doi:10.3389/fneng.2014.00032
McCann H, Pisano G, Beltrachini L (2019). Variation in reported human head tissue electrical conductivity values. Brain Topography 32(5):825–858 doi:10.1007/s10548-019-00710-2

statement: The concentric-sphere head model (brain, CSF, skull, scalp with radii 8.0, 8.1, 8.6, 9.2 cm) is the standard analytic EEG forward model; exact series solutions for arbitrary multilayer spheres are given by de Munck & Peters (1993) and Zhang (1995), and Berg & Scherg (1994) give a fast approximation.
sources: Nunez PL, Nunez MD, Srinivasan R (2019). Multi-scale neural sources of EEG: genuine, equivalent, and representative. A tutorial review. Brain Topography 32(2):193–214 doi:10.1007/s10548-019-00701-3
de Munck JC, Peters MJ (1993). A fast method to compute the potential in the multisphere model. IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering 40(11):1166–1174 doi:10.1109/10.245635
Zhang Z (1995). A fast method to compute surface potentials generated by dipoles within multilayer anisotropic spheres. Physics in Medicine and Biology 40(3):335–349 doi:10.1088/0031-9155/40/3/001

Berg P, Scherg M (1994). A fast method for forward computation of multiple-shell spherical head models. Electroencephalography and Clinical Neurophysiology 90(1):58–64 doi:10.1016/0013-4694(94)90113-9

statement: Eye blinks occur about 12–18 times per minute, with spectral content mainly below ~15 Hz, strongest at frontal electrodes.
sources: Ronca V, Capotorto R, Di Flumeri G, et al. (2024). Optimizing EEG signal integrity: a comprehensive guide to ocular artifact correction. Bioengineering 11(10):1018 doi:10.3390/bioengineering11101018

statement: Averaging N trials improves the signal-to-noise ratio of an event-related potential in proportion to √N; typical components are a few microvolts (error-related negativity 5–15 µV, lateralised readiness potential 1–4 µV) while single-trial noise is much larger than the signal.
sources: Boudewyn MA, Luck SJ, Farrens JL, Kappenman ES (2018). How many trials does it take to get a significant ERP effect? It depends. Psychophysiology 55(6):e13049 doi:10.1111/psyp.13049

statement: Non-contact electrodes couple through tens of picofarads, insulated electrodes in direct skin contact through ~300 pF to several nF; a custom amplifier reached 50 TΩ ∥ 60 fF input impedance and worked with coupling capacitances as low as 0.5 pF; a practical active electrode has ~5 pF input capacitance which forms a divider with the coupling capacitance unless actively shielded.
sources: Chi YM, Jung T-P, Cauwenberghs G (2010). Dry-contact and noncontact biopotential electrodes: methodological review. IEEE Reviews in Biomedical Engineering 3:106–119 doi:10.1109/RBME.2010.2084078

Chi YM, Maier C, Cauwenberghs G (2011). Ultra-high input impedance, low noise integrated amplifier for noncontact biopotential sensing. IEEE Journal on Emerging and Selected Topics in Circuits and Systems 1(4):526–535 doi:10.1109/JETCAS.2011.2179419
Taheri BA, Knight RT, Smith RL (1994). A dry electrode for EEG recording. Electroencephalography and Clinical Neurophysiology 90(5):376–383 doi:10.1016/0013-4694(94)90053-1

statement: Generalised spatial-frequency analysis of a realistic four-compartment head model: about 110 spatial-frequency components capture 99% of the scalp-EEG topography energy of the most superficial sources (versus ~300 for on-scalp MEG), requiring an EEG sensor spacing of ~2.6 cm (~120 sensors); without a skull the count rises to 300–350.
sources: Iivanainen J, Mäkinen AJ, Zetter R, Stenroos M, Ilmoniemi RJ, Parkkonen L (2021). Spatial sampling of MEG and EEG based on generalized spatial-frequency analysis and optimal design. NeuroImage 245:118747 (preprint arXiv:1912.05401) doi:10.1016/j.neuroimage.2021.118747

statement: The adult human brain contains 86 ± 8 billion neurons, of which 19% (about 16 billion) are in the cerebral cortex.
sources: Azevedo FAC, Carvalho LRB, Grinberg LT, et al. (2009). Equal numbers of neuronal and nonneuronal cells make the human brain an isometrically scaled-up primate brain. Journal of Comparative Neurology 513(5):532–541 doi:10.1002/cne.21974
